outputs.L1:
Ito ran to a window. He danced.
He howled. He cursed the moon,
interned within a camp before he was
carted aboard a ship back to Tokyo.
Had he not almost died for art
those evenings he supped on bread soup?
If he wished to forget those days
and nights spent dancing in the drawing rooms
of London, or translating Fenollosa's
notes on Noh, he would have to unbraid
himself from *At the Hawk's Well*,
and then release the Egyptian
mask that Dulac painted him into—
claws, beak, feathers, and legend.
Why did that foolish boy recount a tale
of his grandmother weeping
when first she saw him clad
in his grandfather's samurai armor
to hold the gaze of Lady Cunard?
Once more he was studying the fox,
holding a biscuit in his hand,
saying, "I went to a great hill
in Hampstead and I made my soul
into the soul of a fox." At last,
he would relinquish his Europe,
and not dwell on those he loved
and taught, Isadora lost. Now,
powerless and alone, he dances
his ten steps again and again,
longing to know whether a hawk
could peck the eyes out of a fox.

# The Final Chapter of Ito's Life

Ito's journey took a devastating turn when he was interned in a camp and subsequently deported by ship back to Tokyo. This forced departure marked the end of his life abroad, severing the connections he had cultivated over years spent developing his craft in foreign lands.

His dedication to his art had never been without sacrifice. Throughout his struggling years, Ito endured profound poverty and hardship, surviving on meager meals such as bread soup. These lean times were the price he paid for his artistic pursuits, a testament to the depth of his commitment even when material comfort remained out of reach.

Ito's artistic legacy was inextricably bound to his performances. Among his most significant contributions was his involvement in W.B. Yeats's "At the Hawk's Well," as well as his important work translating Fenollosa's notes on Noh theater. Through these endeavors, he helped bridge Eastern and Western artistic traditions, leaving an indelible mark on the theatrical world.

In his later reflections, Ito sought to release himself from his European past. This meant letting go not only of the places he had known but also of the people who had shaped his life—those he had loved and those he had taught, including the celebrated dancer Isadora Duncan. It was a painful process of severing ties with a chapter of his life that had once defined him.

Now rendered powerless and isolated, Ito found himself trapped in a haunting repetition. He compulsively performed his ten dance steps, over and over, while contemplating a disturbing image: that of a hawk destroying a fox. This vivid, unsettling vision seemed to capture something essential about his diminished state—a once-vibrant artist reduced to solitary ritual, haunted by images of predation and loss.

# The Hawk and the Fox

The old man sits in a small room in Tokyo, and the city outside is not the city he remembers, nor is it the city he ever wanted. Michio Ito—dancer, once the toast of London drawing rooms and Parisian salons—has come home, though "home" is a word that no longer fits him properly, like a costume tailored for another body. He was interned when the war made an enemy of his face, and then deported across an ocean to a country that had become foreign to him in his long absence. Now he waits, and remembers, and the two acts have become nearly the same.

The memories arrive not in sequence but in fragments, as light comes through a shutter. There is Yeats, gaunt and passionate, and the strange hushed premiere of *At the Hawk's Well*, where Ito had moved as the Guardian of the Well, his body folded into the geometry of a hawk. He had worn the mask; he had become the bird that watches over waters that never quench. He remembers the London evenings afterward, the murmur of admiration, the way the English aristocracy had leaned toward him as toward something exotic and rare. He remembers bending over the Noh manuscripts, translating the old notations, explaining to poets and painters the codified gestures of a theater centuries old—teaching the West to read a language written in the body.

All of this had been his life, and all of it is gone.

He cannot let it go. That is the tragedy the poem circles. Powerless now, without stage or audience or the delicate machinery of fame, he rehearses his dance alone in the empty room. The hawk returns to him, and with it the fox—those recurring emblems that stalk through his mind: the hunter and the hunted, the wild thing and the cunning thing, the predator that soars and the creature that slinks close to the earth. Perhaps he is both. Perhaps the fox is what he has become, driven to ground, while the hawk is what he was, high and untouchable in the theatrical air.

He lifts his arms. The gesture is precise; his body still knows what his circumstances have forgotten. But there is no one to see, and the dance dissolves into the small room, into the ordinary afternoon, into a Tokyo that does not care that he once held Europe in his open palm.

And so the poem gathers its themes into this single trembling figure: the exile who carries a lost world inside him, the artist for whom memory is both refuge and wound, and the cost—always the cost—of a life given wholly to art. To have made beauty, and to have been discarded. To have been the hawk, and to end as the fox, rehearsing the old flight in a room where no wings can open.

# A Day in Tokyo

Ito had lived in Tokyo his entire life, yet the city never ceased to surprise him. Each morning, as he walked through the crowded streets of Shibuya, he discovered something new—a tucked-away café, an unfamiliar alley, or a stranger's kind smile.

On this particular day, Ito realized he hadn't visited the quieter neighborhoods in years. Tokyo, for all its neon lights and rushing trains, held pockets of peaceful stillness that most tourists never noticed. He decided to explore.

Wandering away from the bustle, Ito found himself near a small temple. He hadn't expected such tranquility so close to the heart of the metropolis. The gentle sound of a bell echoed through the courtyard, and for a moment, the noise of Tokyo faded completely.

"I hadn't remembered how beautiful this place was," Ito thought, pausing to breathe in the crisp air.

As the sun began to set over Tokyo's endless skyline, Ito made a quiet promise to himself: he wouldn't let the busy pace of city life keep him from these hidden treasures again. Tokyo was more than skyscrapers and technology—it was history, silence, and unexpected moments of grace, waiting patiently for anyone willing to slow down and look.

Ito smiled and continued on his way, grateful for a city that always had more to offer.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about Michio Ito, the Japanese dancer who worked with W.B. Yeats on "At the Hawk's Well," reflecting on his internment during WWII and deportation to Japan.
counterfactuals.output:
# For Michio Ito

In London's fog you found the hawk,
its wings a shadow Yeats could hear—
the well gone dry, the guardian's stalk,
the dance that made the myth appear.

Your body spoke what words could not,
the Noh's slow breath in Western air,
Dulac's masks, the measured plot,
you moved between two worlds with care.

Then Hollywood, the dream machine,
you shaped in bodies light and stone,
choreographed the space between
the cultures you had made your own.

But December's fire changed the sky—
a name, a face, became a crime.
They took you where the fences lie,
your art suspended out of time.

Behind the wire, what dances died?
What gestures held against the cold?
The country that you dignified
now marked you, bartered, bought and sold.

Deported to a homeland's shore
you'd left so many years before,
a stranger twice, on either side,
the ocean wide, the ocean wide.

Yet still I see the hawk take flight,
your arms describing ancient air—
no nation owns that arc of light,
no border holds a dancer there.

The well runs dry, the guardian sleeps,
but memory, like water, keeps
the shape of everything it wore:
your dance, the myth, the distant shore.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a narrative poem exploring the life of a modernist-era Japanese performer looking back on his years in London and his fall from artistic fame, ending in isolation.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Silk Screen Falls

*I.*

The mirror in this Tokyo room has clouded like my eyes,
and morning finds me small beneath a paper lantern's rise.
They call me *sensei* now—the boy who serves me morning tea—
but I remember London fog, and who I used to be.

*II.*

The year was nineteen-twenty when the great ship carried me
across the churning distances of an indifferent sea.
I brought my father's masks, my mother's careful, folded silk,
and dreams as thin and luminous as skin on cooling milk.

They wanted something *foreign* then, the theaters of the West—
an Orient of gesture that would answer their unrest.
I gave them *Noh* made pliable, I bent tradition's spine
to fit inside their appetite, and called the ruin mine.

*III.*

How London loved me! Bloomsbury would gather at my feet,
the poets and the painters in their scarves along the street.
I danced the crane, the maiden, and the ghost who cannot rest,
and critics wrote in praises that I pressed against my chest.

A woman with pale shoulders and a laugh like breaking glass
would meet me after curtain-fall and walk me through the grass.
She never learned my language but she memorized my face—
*You are not like the others,* she would murmur, *you have grace.*

I was the season's marvel, I was everyone's delight,
a lacquered thing that glittered in the gaslight of the night.
I did not see the hunger in their soft, applauding hands—
they loved the mask I offered, not the man who understands.

*IV.*

The fashions turn like weather. What is worshipped fades to quaint.
By nineteen-twenty-nine I was a rumor, then a faint
remembered curiosity, a name misspelled in print—
the *Japanese sensation* now reduced to passing hint.

New dancers filled the theaters, more modern and more raw.
They wanted Freud and fever now, not ceremony's law.
My careful centuries of art, my silence and my snow,
became a thing too delicate for audiences to know.

The woman with pale shoulders married someone from the North.
She sent a card at Christmas, then no more came trembling forth.
The invitations thinned like ice in April's careless thaw,
and I performed to rows of dark, to no one, to the maw.

*V.*

I sold my mother's silk to pay the passage home again,
and folded up my father's masks and all the man I'd been.
The harbor did not know me. Tokyo had changed her face.
The war-clouds gathered eastward and I had no earthly place.

*VI.*

So now I teach the gestures to the boy who brings my tea.
His hands are quick; he does not know what these old hands could be.
I show him how the ghost returns, how sorrow learns to fold—
and something in his patient eyes reminds me I am old.

The London fog has lifted into memory's dim gauze.
I danced for their delight and then I danced for their applause,
and then I danced for empty chairs, and then I did not dance—
and all that famous glitter was a country's brief romance.

*VII.*

The lantern gutters. Outside, snow is settling on the eaves,
as quiet as the dropping of a thousand paper leaves.
I was a screen they painted on, a surface, bright and thin—
and now the silk has fallen, there is only me within.

I hold my father's oldest mask against the failing light.
It has no name, this carven face; it stares into the night.
*We are the same,* I tell it, and I set it by my bed—
two hollow things that outlived all the beautiful things said.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about an artist interned in a WWII camp who reminisces about his glamorous past dancing in European drawing rooms and performing Noh-influenced theater.
counterfactuals.output:
**Behind the Wire, a Dancer Remembers**

The dust here settles like a second skin,
fine as the powder we once brushed
across our faces before the lamps came up—
though now it only greys the barrack boards,
the tin plate, the back of my folded hands.

I was luminous once.

In Vienna, in Paris, the chandeliers
would hush themselves when I entered,
and the women in their long gloves
leaned forward as if I carried
some rumor of the sea.
I danced across their parquet floors
the way a heron steps through shallows—
slow, deliberate, my body
a held breath they were afraid to break.

They did not know the discipline of it.
They saw only the silk,
the way I could pour myself
from stillness into motion
and back to stillness,
the mask of my own face
learning to become
a spirit, a demon, a woman weeping
at the edge of a painted pine.

*Yūgen,* my teacher called it—
that depth beneath the surface,
the grief you cannot point to,
only circle, the way the moon
circles the mountain it cannot touch.

Now the searchlight is my moon.
It sweeps the yard each night
and finds me at the window,
an old man practicing the smallest gesture—
the turn of a wrist,
the lifting of an invisible fan—
so that the guards, if they looked,
would see a fool, a shadow,
some harmless thing
gone soft in the head.

Let them.

They have taken the country I was born to,
the country I made my home,
and left me stranded on the isthmus
of my own two feet.
But they cannot take the arc a hand can carve
through desert air,
cannot confiscate the memory of applause
that broke like surf
in a room a thousand miles and twenty years from here.

So I rehearse.
Barefoot on the splintered floor,
I become the heron again,
the demon, the weeping woman,
each night a little more transparent,
until the wire, the towers, the guns
dissolve into the middle distance—
and I am only movement,
only the held breath
before the lamps come up,
only *yūgen,*
that depth
they were always
too far away
to see.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, allusive poem about identity, exile, and the loss of a European artistic life, featuring the imagery of a hawk, a fox, and a mask.
counterfactuals.output:
# Émigré

The hawk I was hangs framed above the stairs,
a pinned thing, wings spread wide as any door
I cannot walk back through. In Budapest
they knew my name the way one knows a coin—
by weight, by ring, by what it could command.

Here I am fox. I learn the low pursuits,
the doubling-back, the scent laid false across
the snow of an accountant's ledger book.
I have made cunning where I once made art.
The galleries are shuttered in my skull,
their varnished saints gone brown as autumn ponds.

A mask waits in the trunk beneath the bed—
Venetian, cracked, the eyeholes rimmed with gilt.
I wore it once in a palazzo's blaze
where music was a language everyone
was born already speaking. Now I press
its cold interior to my living face
and feel the exile in the fit: too large,
as if the man it shaped had emigrated first
and left the shape to follow, ill-supplied.

The hawk does not forgive the sky its distance.
The fox does not forgive the hawk its fall.
And I, between them, neither wild nor tame,
rehearse a mother tongue to empty rooms
where the words arrive like letters, months delayed,
the sender dead, the address torn away—

and still I read them. Still the varnish holds
one figure in its amber: someone bright,
mid-gesture, reaching for a brush, a bow,
a face that was his own and not a mask,
in a country that was his and is now paint.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a persona poem from the perspective of a dancer named Ito who once collaborated with Yeats and Edmund Dulac, now powerless and rehearsing his old choreography alone.
counterfactuals.output:
**Ito, Rehearsing**

They wanted a hawk and I gave them a hawk,
though I had never watched one—
only the pigeons of London parks
and, in the zoo, one bird that would not turn its head.

Yeats read the lines in a cellar off Cavendish Square.
Dulac hammered gold into a mask
that looked out and saw nothing,
which is the only way a god can look.

I was the Guardian of the Well.
Understand: the well was empty.
The water came three times a lifetime
and I was posted there to make sure
no thirst arrived at the right moment.

I was very good at this.
I could hold a hand the way a branch holds snow—
until the whole room forgot the branch
and believed only in the falling.

Now the room is this room.
The mirror keeps a version of me
who is slower than the version I intend.
I lift the arm. The arm agrees to be lifted.
Something behind the arm does not.

I mark the steps I once flew through—
the drift, the crouch, the sudden opening
that used to make the poet lean forward
as if the water had at last arrived.

The old dead pull their masks back on.
Yeats in his cellar. Dulac at his gold.
And I, who was hired to guard an emptiness,
find I have kept my post too well:

here it is, the guarded thing,
still full of nothing,
and I am dancing toward it
the way the tide practices
its long approach to a coast
it will never be allowed to touch.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
